case_facts: A ride-hailing app shared my phone number and live location with third-party advertisers without my consent. I never agreed to this in their privacy policy.

analysis.summary: A ride-hailing application allegedly shared the user's personal data, including phone number and live location, with third-party advertisers without obtaining informed consent. The user contends that such data sharing was not disclosed or authorized under the platform's privacy policy. This raises concerns of unauthorized processing of sensitive personal data and potential consumer rights violations.

issues.issue: Unauthorized collection and sharing of sensitive personal data including location and phone number without consent
issues.governing_law: Information Technology (Amendment) Act 2008, Section 43A; IT (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules 2011, Rule 5
issues.kanoon_query: sensitive personal data sharing without consent IT Act

issues.issue: Deficiency in service and unfair trade practice by ride-hailing platform for misuse of personal data
issues.governing_law: Consumer Protection Act 2019, Section 2(11) and Section 2(47)
issues.kanoon_query: unfair trade practice data privacy consumer protection

issues.issue: Breach of privacy policy terms constituting a contractual violation and tortious invasion of privacy
issues.kanoon_query: breach privacy policy app user data India

issues.issue: Right to privacy violated by unauthorized disclosure of personal data to third parties
issues.governing_law: Article 21, Constitution of India; Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1
issues.kanoon_query: right to privacy personal data third party disclosure

governing_acts: IT (Reasonable Security Practices and Sensitive Personal Data) Rules 2011

transcript.argument:
Your Lordship, I appear on behalf of the Complainant, a consumer who placed her trust — and her physical safety — in the hands of a ride-hailing platform, only to have that trust shattered by the deliberate, unauthorized sharing of her most sensitive personal data: her live location and phone number, handed over to third-party advertisers without a whisper of consent.

Your Lordship, the facts are stark and unambiguous. The Complainant never agreed, expressly or impliedly, to the sharing of her sensitive personal data with commercial third parties. Rule 5 of the IT (Reasonable Security Practices and Sensitive Personal Data) Rules, 2011 mandates that a body corporate must obtain **prior written consent** before collecting or sharing sensitive personal data, and Rule 6 categorically prohibits disclosure to third parties without such consent. The Respondent violated both provisions in letter and in spirit. A phone number and live location — data that can expose a woman to stalking, harassment, and physical danger — squarely fall within the definition of "sensitive personal data" under these Rules. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 further reinforces this framework, establishing that personal data may only be processed for a **specified, lawful purpose** with the data principal's free and informed consent. No such consent existed here.

Your Lordship, this is equally a consumer dispute of the gravest kind. Under Section 2(11) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, any deficiency in service — including a breach of the duty of confidentiality owed to a consumer — renders the service provider liable. The Respondent's privacy policy, which the Complainant relied upon when engaging the platform, did not authorize third-party commercial sharing. The Respondent therefore committed an **unfair trade practice** under Section 2(47) of the same Act by misrepresenting the nature of its data-handling practices. The Complainant is entitled to compensation for the mental agony, loss of privacy, and the very real physical risk she was exposed to. I would draw Your Lordship's attention to the principle recognized in *Anantha Murthy A.S. v. Reserve Bank of India* (docid: 68585959), where the Central Information Commission explicitly held that disclosure of personal and sensitive information **without the consent** of the data subject constitutes a breach of customer trust and causes demonstrable harm — a principle that applies with full force to the Respondent's conduct here.

Your Lordship, the Respondent cannot hide behind fine print it never disclosed, nor can it monetize a consumer's vulnerability for advertising revenue. We shall demonstrate through evidence that the sharing was systematic, intentional, and profitable for the Respondent — aggravating factors that this Hon'ble Forum must weigh while awarding compensation. We seek a declaration of deficiency in service, an injunction against further data sharing, and substantial compensatory and punitive damages. The law is clear; the facts are undisputed; justice demands accountability.
